prompt: Why can the entropy change of a chemical reaction be calculated from tabulated standard entropies of the reactants and products, whatever path the reaction actually takes?

choices.text: Entropy is a state function
Entropy is conserved in every reaction
choices.why: Entropy is not conserved; Δ_rxn S° is usually nonzero. The method works because S depends only on the state, not on the path.

choices.text: Every chemical reaction is reversible
choices.why: Most real reactions are irreversible. The calculation still works because S is a state function, so any path between the same states gives the same ΔS.

choices.text: The reaction is assumed to take place at 0 K
choices.why: Standard entropies are tabulated at a fixed temperature such as 298 K, not 0 K. The method works because S is a state function.

explanation: Because S is a state function, ΔS depends only on the initial and final states. So the difference between the products' and reactants' standard entropies gives Δ_rxn S°, however the reaction is actually carried out.

prompt: Which expression gives the standard entropy change of a reaction, Δ_rxn S°, from standard molar entropies S° and stoichiometric coefficients ν?

choices.text: Σν S°(products) − Σν S°(reactants)
Σν S°(reactants) − Σν S°(products)
choices.why: That is the reverse, which gives the entropy change for the reaction run backwards. The section takes products minus reactants.

choices.text: Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants), ignoring the ν
choices.why: Each S° is per mole, so it must be multiplied by the number of moles in the balanced equation. Leaving out ν gives the wrong answer whenever a coefficient isn't 1.

choices.text: Σν S°(products) + Σν S°(reactants)
choices.why: A change is a difference, final minus initial, not a sum. Subtract the reactants' sum from the products' sum.

explanation: Δ_rxn S° = Σν S°(products) − Σν S°(reactants), where each ν is the species' coefficient in the balanced equation. It is the entropy of the final state minus that of the initial state.

prompt: In the methane combustion, O2 is an element in its standard state, yet its S° of 205.15 J/(mol·K) still counts twice in the reactants' sum. Why isn't it taken as zero?

choices.text: S° is an absolute entropy, and O2's is above zero
Its standard enthalpy of formation is also nonzero
choices.why: ΔH°_f of O2 is zero by convention, yet its S° is not. Entropies sit on an absolute scale set by the third law, so elements have positive S°.

choices.text: Gases are never set to zero, only solid elements
choices.why: Solid elements have positive S° at 298 K too. S° values are absolute entropies, zero only for a perfect crystal at 0 K.

choices.text: Its entry corrects for the heat the reaction releases
choices.why: S° values are entropies, not heats, and the heat of reaction does not enter Δ_rxn S°. O2 counts because its absolute entropy at 298 K is above zero.

explanation: Unlike enthalpies, entropies have a natural zero: a perfect crystal at 0 K. Every substance at 298 K, element or compound, has a positive S°, so O2 contributes 2 × 205.15 = 410.30 J/(mol·K) to the reactants' sum.

prompt: For CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → 2H2O(g) + CO2(g), the standard entropies are 186.25 J/(mol·K) for CH4, 205.15 J/(mol·K) for O2, 188.84 J/(mol·K) for H2O(g) and 213.79 J/(mol·K) for CO2. What is Δ_rxn S°, in J/(mol·K)? (Give it as a decimal.)
A reaction has a negative Δ_rxn S°. What does the sign tell you?

choices.text: Products hold less entropy than reactants
The reaction cannot happen on its own
choices.why: The sign of the system's ΔS alone does not decide spontaneity; heat given to the surroundings also raises their entropy. The minus sign only says the products' entropy is lower.

choices.text: The reaction must absorb heat
choices.why: Δ_rxn S° says nothing directly about heat flow; many reactions with negative Δ_rxn S° release heat. The minus sign means the products have less entropy.

choices.text: Entropy is destroyed, which breaks the second law
choices.why: The second law limits the entropy of an isolated system, not of the reacting system alone. The surroundings can gain more entropy than the system loses.

explanation: Δ_rxn S° = Σν S°(products) − Σν S°(reactants), so a negative value means the products, in their standard states, have less entropy than the reactants. Whether the reaction runs on its own also depends on the surroundings.

prompt: In methane combustion, 3 mol of gas, 1 mol of CH4 and 2 mol of O2, turns into 3 mol of gas, 2 mol of H2O and 1 mol of CO2. All four standard entropies lie between about 186 and 214 J/(mol·K). What does this suggest about Δ_rxn S°?

choices.text: It is small, since the two sums nearly cancel
It is large and positive, since a flame is disordered
choices.why: Δ_rxn S° compares the standard entropies of products and reactants, not the look of a flame. The two sums are both near 590 J/(mol·K), so they nearly cancel.

choices.text: It is exactly zero, since the moles of gas match
choices.why: Equal moles of gas make Δ_rxn S° small, not exactly zero, because the S° values still differ a little. The two sums nearly cancel.

choices.text: It is large and negative, since O2 is used up
choices.why: Using up O2 lowers the entropy only as far as the products fail to replace it. The two sums are nearly equal, so Δ_rxn S° is small.

explanation: Three moles of gas with S° near 200 J/(mol·K) on each side give two sums of almost the same size, both close to 590 J/(mol·K). Their difference, Δ_rxn S°, is therefore only a few J/(mol·K).

prompt: In the methane combustion, CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → 2H2O(g) + CO2(g), why is the standard entropy of H2O(g) counted twice in the products' sum?

choices.text: The balanced equation forms 2 mol of H2O
Water has two hydrogen atoms
choices.why: The coefficient comes from the balanced equation, not from the formula. CH4 has four H atoms but is counted once, because 1 mol of it reacts.

choices.text: Water counts once as gas and once as liquid
choices.why: The section uses only H2O(g), with S° = 188.84 J/(mol·K). It is doubled because the balanced equation forms 2 mol of water.

choices.text: Every product is counted twice
choices.why: CO2 is a product too, but it is counted once. Each S° is multiplied by its own coefficient ν in the balanced equation.

explanation: Each S° is a molar entropy, so it is multiplied by the number of moles in the balanced equation, its coefficient ν. The combustion forms 2 mol of H2O and 1 mol of CO2.

prompt: The section's methane combustion makes water vapour, H2O(g), with S° = 188.84 J/(mol·K). Liquid water, H2O(ℓ), has S° = 69.95 J/(mol·K). If the products were CO2(g) and liquid water instead, how would Δ_rxn S° change?

choices.text: It would become much more negative
It would not change, since water is water
choices.why: The phase matters: liquid water has far less entropy than water vapour. With two moles of it among the products, Δ_rxn S° falls a lot.

choices.text: It would become positive
choices.why: Swapping in the lower S° of liquid water shrinks the products' sum, pushing Δ_rxn S° further below zero, not above it.

choices.text: It would become slightly less negative
choices.why: Liquid water has less entropy than vapour, so the products' sum drops. Δ_rxn S° becomes much more negative, not less.

explanation: Each mole of water as liquid has 188.84 − 69.95 = 118.89 J/(mol·K) less entropy than as vapour. With 2 mol of water, the products' sum falls by about 238 J/(mol·K), so Δ_rxn S° becomes strongly negative.

prompt: For 2NO2(g) → N2O4(g), Δ_rxn S° = −175.8 J/(mol·K). What is Δ_rxn S° for the reverse reaction, N2O4(g) → 2NO2(g)?

choices.why: Reversing a reaction swaps products and reactants, so the sign of Δ_rxn S° flips. The reverse reaction has +175.8 J/(mol·K).

choices.text: Zero, since S is a state function
choices.why: Because S is a state function, the forward and reverse changes cancel only over the round trip, so each is the negative of the other. The reverse is +175.8 J/(mol·K).
Reversing a reaction does not double its entropy change; only the sign changes. The reverse reaction has +175.8 J/(mol·K).

explanation: Reversing the reaction swaps the products' and reactants' sums in Δ_rxn S°, so only the sign changes: +175.8 J/(mol·K). Splitting each N2O4 molecule into two NO2 molecules raises the entropy.

prompt: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) → 2NH3(g), the standard entropies are 191.61 J/(mol·K) for N2, 130.68 J/(mol·K) for H2 and 192.77 J/(mol·K) for NH3. What is Δ_rxn S°, in J/(mol·K)? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: Products: 2(192.77) = 385.54. Reactants: 191.61 + 3(130.68) = 583.65. Δ_rxn S° = 385.54 − 583.65 = −198.11 J/(mol·K); 4 mol of gas become 2 mol, so the entropy falls.

prompt: For CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g), the standard entropies are 91.7 J/(mol·K) for CaCO3(s), 38.1 J/(mol·K) for CaO(s) and 213.8 J/(mol·K) for CO2(g). What is Δ_rxn S°, in J/(mol·K)? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: Δ_rxn S° = (38.1 + 213.8) − 91.7 = 251.9 − 91.7 = 160.2 J/(mol·K). It is large and positive because the reaction releases a gas, CO2, whose S° is far above that of either solid.
